title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The World of Mutual Benefit and Hidden Identities

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, careful, and occasionally heated conversation about one of the greatest novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend is Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is — by almost any measure — his most ambitious.
It is a novel about money, about identity worn and discarded like a coat, about what society does to the people it has decided to throw away.
And it begins, characteristically, with a dead man floating in a river — and a very grand dinner party.
Joining me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel, each of whom brings a genuinely different set of eyes to the text.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has recorded more classic novels for the ear than almost anyone alive — he hears the rhythms of this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is first and foremost a moral inquiry — into character, goodness, and failure.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he will not let us look away from what this novel shows us about who pays the price.
We begin where Dickens himself begins — not with a hero, but with a world.
A world built, literally and figuratively, out of dust.
And Dickens announces that world with a kind of comic bravado that I find completely irresistible.
We're at this elegant dinner party, and Mortimer Lightwood is telling the story of old Harmon — the Dust Contractor — and he does it with this magnificent, deadpan accumulation.
Listen to how Dickens writes the actual wealth of this man.
"Coal-dust, vegetable-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust, rough dust and sifted dust, — all manner of Dust."
That final capitalised "Dust" — it's not an accident on the page, and it should never be an accident in the mouth.
Dickens has just told you that this entire novel's inheritance — its fortune, its tragedy, its social machinery — is composed of other people's rubbish.
And he's done it with a list that makes you laugh before it makes you think.
Oliver is right that the comedy is doing serious work — though I'd frame what that work is rather differently.
The Dust Contractor is not primarily a symbol of capitalism, nor a satirical target of any political system.
He is a study in a particular deformation of character — a man who has made his entire selfhood out of acquisition, and thereby hollowed himself out.
The image is perfectly chosen: a man who lives in a hollow of his own making, on an estate that Dickens describes as a mountain range thrown up like an old volcano.
Dust was the old man's god, and it consumed him as surely as it will consume us all.
That is a moral observation — and a deeply traditional one — before it is anything else.
Edmund's reading is eloquent, and I don't entirely quarrel with it — but it stops at the individual when the novel is clearly pointing elsewhere.
The Dust Contractor's fortune is not a parable about greed in the abstract — it is a precise account of how Victorian capitalism actually worked.
The dust heap was a real thing — a site where the detritus of the city was sorted, sold, recycled back into the economy by the very poorest workers.
And old Harmon got rich by owning that process — by owning, in effect, other people's labour over other people's waste.
When Dickens lists all those dusts — coal-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust — he is listing the materials of actual working lives.
The comedy and the horror are inseparable in that sentence — and that, I'd argue, is Dickens at his most radical.
Daniel, I think you're absolutely right that the comedy and the horror are fused — and the way Dickens fuses them is through his prose style, which is itself a kind of performance.
Consider the passage where Dickens sets the scene for a foggy London day — and I mean one of the great set-pieces of descriptive prose in the language.

"Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither."
"Animate" and "inanimate" — that is the whole novel in two words.
The fog blurs the line between the living and the dead, between the person and the system that surrounds them.
And that collapsing sun — gone out, flat, cold — that's not decoration.
That is Dickens telling you what kind of world his characters have been born into.
There I find myself in genuine agreement with Oliver — the fog passage is extraordinary, and precisely because it isn't merely atmospheric.
The movement from grey fog to yellow to brown to rusty-black — towards the heart of the City — is a moral gradient, not just a meteorological one.
The closer one gets to the centre of commercial power, the darker and more suffocating the air becomes.
One may read that as politics if one wishes — but it is equally, and more essentially, a vision of spiritual condition.
Dickens is not mapping class — he is mapping the human cost of a world in which wealth has displaced every other value.
And when Dickens moves from that fog-enveloped City to the riverbank, the social mapping becomes even more explicit.
There is a passage — the carriage ride down through Ratcliffe and Rotherhithe — where Dickens simply states what the geography of poverty means.
"Accumulated scum of humanity seemed to be washed from higher grounds, like so much moral sewage, and to be pausing until its own weight forced it over the bank and sunk it in the river."
The phrase "moral sewage" is devastating — and we need to be clear about what Dickens is doing with it.
He is not saying the poor are moral sewage — he is reporting how the prosperous classes perceive them, and making the reader feel the obscenity of that perception.
The geography does the ideological work: wealth flows up, poverty drains down, and the river is at the bottom, receiving everything the city cannot bear to see.
That is not a metaphor — that is the structure of Victorian London, described with surgical precision.
What strikes me about that carriage ride is the rhythm of it — "In and out among vessels that seemed to have got ashore, and houses that seemed to have got afloat."
The world is inverted down here — ships and houses have swapped places, nothing is where it ought to be.
And then the wheels simply stop — at a dark corner, river-washed and otherwise not washed at all.
That final clause is Dickens's dark joke landing right on the beat — and it's a joke that makes you wince rather than laugh.
Dust, fog, and the river — Dickens has established his world in the first pages with extraordinary efficiency.
And into this world he places his characters — people who must negotiate what money does to the soul, and what happens when you choose to refuse it.
Which brings us to one of the novel's most extraordinary arcs — a young woman who begins the book in love with wealth, and ends it having discovered something far more difficult to value.
After the break, we turn to Bella Wilfer — and to the question of what it actually costs to become yourself.

segments.title: The Art of Becoming: Bella's Reckoning with Money and Self

utterances.text: We've been talking about how this novel hides its true workings — false identities, concealed inheritances, a world where almost no one is quite who they seem.
But there is one character whose hidden identity is not imposed from outside — it has to be forged from within: Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a self-confessed mercenary — and ends it having chosen, at real cost, not to be.
Oliver, she's your kind of character — someone written for the voice, for the stage almost. Where does her arc begin for you?
Bella is one of those characters where Dickens is performing a high-wire act from the very first scene she appears in.
He needs us to like her enough to follow her — but also to see, quite clearly, that she is vain, greedy, and thoroughly confused about what she wants.
And the key to all of that is the mirror. She keeps addressing herself in the looking-glass — holding herself to account in the most theatrical way possible.
There's this extraordinary passage where she has just heard Mr Boffin say exactly what she herself has always believed about money — and she finds she can't bear it.
"Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself."
And then — the punchline she delivers to her own reflection:
"Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?"
The comedy is impeccable — but Dickens has also, in that word 'Beast,' slipped in something genuinely uncomfortable.
What strikes me about that scene is what it tells us about the architecture of moral self-knowledge in Dickens.
Bella does not need to be told she is wrong — she already knows. The problem is that knowing and feeling are operating on entirely separate tracks.
This is, in the end, a novel about the education of the will — not the intellect.
Dickens understands that you cannot think your way to virtue. You have to be formed by experience — by suffering, if necessary.
And that night, after this little self-interrogation, what does the novel give us?
"A weariness upon her spirit which was more than the weariness of want of sleep."
That is not comic at all. That is a soul beginning, very slowly, to grieve for what it has been.
I want to hold on to that mirror image for a moment, because I think it's doing more than comic business.
Bella interrogates herself in the looking-glass — which is a polished surface that shows you yourself as a commodity, as an image to be assessed and marketed.
She has grown up knowing her value is entirely determined by the marriage market. Of course she measures herself in a mirror.
Now, what I find genuinely radical in this novel is that Dickens refuses to let Boffin's corruption be merely personal.
When Bella finally understands the lesson she's been taught, she articulates it with remarkable precision.

"This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in; but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking."
A glaring instance. Wealth displayed in its most degraded form, as a deliberate pedagogical strategy.
Dickens is saying: you cannot simply tell the comfortable classes what money does to people. You must show them. And they still might not see it.
That pedagogical framing is fascinating — but what I love about Bella is that she doesn't learn the lesson tidily. She fights it.
And when she does finally arrive at her moral resolution, Dickens gives it to us via her father — the beloved Cherub — in this wonderfully oblique, self-deprecating way.
The old man reports on his daughter as though he can barely believe she is his:

"this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive."
'Distantly related to myself.' He can't quite own her — she has become too extraordinary for him to quite claim.
The comedy carries the emotion. As it almost always does in Dickens at his best.
What that passage also makes clear is that Bella's transformation is not a conversion to selflessness — it is a conversion to integrity.
She does not become poor, or ascetic, or indifferent to comfort. She becomes someone who refuses to sell her moral sense.
That is a very specific, very classical virtue — it corresponds quite precisely to what the ancients called constancy.
And Dickens is not satisfied with showing us the moment of decision. He insists on testing it.
Bella herself demands to be tested — which is really quite remarkable for a character who began the novel demanding only comfort and luxury.
"Try me through some reverse, John — try me through some trial — and tell them after that, what you think of me."
She is asking to be proved. Not merely to feel changed, but to be known to have changed.
That line lodges in the mind precisely because it upends every expectation the novel has built around her.
But I want to push back, gently, on reading this purely as personal moral growth.
Bella's transformation is only possible because someone with resources — Boffin — orchestrates an elaborate deception to force it.
The girl without a fortune cannot simply choose virtue in a vacuum. She has to be placed in conditions that make virtue thinkable.
Dickens understood something important there, even if he couldn't quite say it directly: that moral life is also a product of material circumstance.
Bella's education, then, is also a kind of indictment — of what wealth does to people, and of the conditions under which it becomes possible to refuse it.

Which brings us, inevitably, to the source of all this wealth — the dust heaps themselves, and what Dickens makes of the Victorian obsession with money, refuse, and the uncomfortable proximity of the two.

segments.title: The Dust Heap Rises: Wealth, Filth, and Victorian Reckoning

utterances.text: We've been tracking Bella Wilfer's complicated education in the meaning of money.
But Dickens isn't only asking what wealth does to one person — he's asking what it does to an entire society.
In this segment, we turn to the dust heap itself — that extraordinary symbol at the novel's heart — and to the system of charity, parasitism, and institutional cruelty that surrounds it.
You know, before we get to the grand systemic arguments, I want to linger on a single passage that I think is among the funniest things Dickens ever put on a page.
It's the moment the Secretary opens Boffin's correspondence — the flood of charitable appeals that descend the instant a man is known to have money.
Dickens lists them with this glorious, almost musical accumulation:

'Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred children to be brought up on postage stamps.'
The comedy is in the descending coin — half-crowns down to postage stamps — and in that final absurdity, children raised on stamps.
It is a list that could only be read aloud, and Dickens knew it.
The comic cataloguing is exquisite — I grant you that entirely, Oliver.
But what strikes me is the character study underneath the satire.
Boffin himself is not corrupted by this correspondence — he employs a Secretary precisely because he has the good sense to know his own limitations.
And then there is the Duke of Linseed — the letter that is all warm intimacy and entirely lithographed by the hundred.
Dickens gives us the postscript with particular relish:
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
The adjectives do all the work — four of them before we even get to the letter itself.
Dickens knows that self-importance inflates language before it inflates anything else.
The comedy is real, but I'd want us to hold it against something harder.
What the Secretary's letters reveal is a philanthropic economy — a market in good causes where the currency is social visibility, not relief.
The Duke of Linseed is not giving money; he is selling Boffin an association with aristocratic prestige.
And that three-guinea steward's fee is the transaction laid bare — Boffin pays; the Duke's name appears; the poor, if they appear at all, appear in the small print.
Dickens makes it comic because the alternative — stating it plainly — would be too bleak even for him.
And then Dickens gives us Boffin himself in that mansion, and the image he reaches for is — magnificent.
He says the great house was, for Boffin,
'like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.'
A cheese.
The entire aristocratic tradition of the English country house — summed up as a very large cheese that has gone off.
And yet Boffin simply accepts it as a sort of Legacy Duty — good-natured, enduring, faintly baffled.
That cheese simile is a perfect instance of Dickens's method — the comic image that is also a moral diagnosis.
The parasites are real — we've met them in the Duke's letter and the forty-seven charities before him.
But Boffin's response — resignation as a form of grace — is the novel's quiet praise of an essentially decent man.
Dickens frames it as the Golden Dustman at home — the minion of fortune who is simply not destroyed by fortune.
That is not a small thing in a novel where money unmakes almost everyone it touches.
And yet the novel keeps asking whether even Boffin's decency survives the furnace.
There's a chapter where the narrator poses the question with a terrifying directness:
'Was the Golden Dustman passing through the furnace of proof and coming out dross?'
Dross — the waste skimmed off molten metal.
The image is drawn from the dust heap itself — from the whole economy of sorting and waste that produced Boffin's fortune.
Dickens is asking whether wealth is a refining fire or a corrupting one.
And crucially, it's Bella's perception that is also on trial in that question — can she see clearly, or has money already blurred her vision?
The novel doesn't let you settle into the comedy for very long before it does something like this.
Three sentences — that's the whole chapter opening.
'Were Bella Wilfer's bright and ready little wits at fault... Ill news travels fast. We shall know full soon.'
That last sentence — 'We shall know full soon' — is Dickens the showman, pulling the audience forward by the collar.
He's not a Victorian novelist, he's a Victorian serial writer — and every installment has to leave you reaching for the next one.
Daniel, I find myself in an unusual position — I want to follow your argument about institutional failure, and I want to resist it simultaneously.
Because the great passage you have in front of you — that furious address to the lords and gentlemen and honourable boards — is undeniably polemical.
And yet what Dickens is defending there is not a programme — it is a principle.
He says the truth he's stating has been the truth 'since the foundations of the universe were laid.'
That is not a manifesto — that is a moral absolute.
And that is precisely where I think the novel is more radical than even Dickens consciously intended.
Let me read the passage, because the language earns everything I want to say about it.

'When we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance.'
'The best of the poor detest our mercies' — that is the devastating phrase.
Not the ungrateful poor — the best of them.
Dickens is saying that the charitable system actively repels the people it claims to serve — that its design is as much about control as relief.
Edmund, that is not merely a moral absolute — it is a structural diagnosis.
And it's given flesh — literal, physical, devastating flesh — in Betty Higden.
Betty is the embodiment of exactly the person Dickens means by 'the best of the poor.'
She walks herself to death rather than enter the workhouse.
And in her wanderings, Dickens shows us what she encounters at every turn — including this figure:
'the appointed evader of the public trust did his dirty office of trying to weary them out and so get rid of them.'
'His dirty office.' Dickens gives the bureaucrat his job title and then names it honestly.
I will not defend the workhouse system — no one with any humanity could.
But I want to note what makes Betty Higden so morally powerful in Dickens's hands — it is not her victimhood.
It is her will.
She acts, she decides, she flees — and in doing so she becomes the sharpest possible rebuke to the system Dickens is attacking.
A purely structural account of her situation, I would suggest, actually diminishes what Dickens achieves by making her a person rather than a case.
I don't think structural and individual are opposites here — Betty's individual will is what the system is specifically designed to break.
The passage makes that explicit — the Union Houses are built as far from home as the county jail, and compared to them unfavorably.
The remoteness is the punishment — separation from community, from memory, from self.
And then — and this is Dickens at his most biting — she hears the Registrar General's reports read aloud:

'the Registrar General cast up the units that had within the last week died of want and of exposure to the weather: for which that Recording Angel seemed to have a regular fixed place in his sum, as if they were its halfpence.'
Deaths as units.
Accounted for as halfpence in a ledger.
Dickens arrives at the logic of the dust heap from the opposite direction — the human beings sorted out as waste.
There is something almost unbearable about the phrase 'as if they were its halfpence' — because halfpence have appeared already, in that comic catalogue of charitable asks.
The novel echoes its own vocabulary — the currency of charity becomes the currency of death — and I'm not sure Dickens always plants that consciously, but the novel finds it anyway.
That is what a great novel does — it thinks more than its author.
We've moved from the comic parasites in Boffin's postbag to Betty Higden dying by the roadside — and what's remarkable is how the same novel holds both without flinching.
The wealth that generates the comedy and the poverty that generates the tragedy are two faces of the same dust heap.

After the break, we'll look at the man who set the whole inheritance in motion — and at the extraordinary narrative cunning Dickens deploys to keep us guessing about John Harmon's true identity and purpose.

segments.title: Harmon's Shadow: Plot, Deception, and Narrative Cunning

utterances.text: We've been talking about how wealth in this novel corrupts everything it touches — the dust heaps, the money, the people who orbit it.
But Dickens has another game running beneath all of that — one of the most audacious deceptions in Victorian fiction.
I want us to look closely at John Harmon — the dead man who isn't dead, the secretary who isn't a secretary, the ghost haunting his own inheritance.
You have to start with the sheer theatrical pleasure of it — the man peeling off his disguise in a deserted street.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary sentence, and I want to read it because no paraphrase does it justice.
"became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world"
And then — almost in the same breath — Rokesmith is also as like Julius Handford as never man was like another.
Three men. One body. The same sentence applies to all three simultaneously.
That is a conjuror's trick — and Dickens lands it with total confidence.
The theatrical pleasure is real — but there's something more unsettling underneath it.
Harmon doesn't just choose to disappear on a whim — the decision is made in a sickbed, in a kind of fever logic.
Dickens tells us exactly what was running through his mind when the idea struck him.
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella"
To prove Bella. That is the phrase that arrests me.
This man will submit a woman to a prolonged test of character — without her knowledge, without her consent — because he doesn't trust what his father's money has made of the world around him.
The inheritance poisons even the act of falling in love. That is precisely Dickens's point.
Dr. Rosen frames this as a structural complaint against Harmon, and I understand the instinct — but I think it misreads the moral texture of the passage.
Dickens is at considerable pains to explain exactly why Harmon's first deception was not cynical.
The passage is worth attending to carefully.

"When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days."
'Never yet for good within his knowledge then.' That small phrase carries an enormous weight.
Harmon has never witnessed his father's wealth doing anything but harm — not malice, but a kind of trained moral blindness.
The deception begins as a form of self-defence by a man who has never been permitted to trust anyone.
Edmund is absolutely right that the novel is sympathetic to Harmon — but what astonishes me as a performer is how Dickens finds the Gothic register to describe a man burying himself.
There is this extraordinary image — the man lying awake all night performing, as Dickens puts it, a 'sexton-task.'

"No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place."
He's not running a con. He has literally become his own ghost.
And then — and this is the detail that kills me — the following morning only deepens it.
"Thus John Rokesmith in the morning, and it buried John Harmon still many fathoms deeper than he had been buried in the night."
Many fathoms deeper. He measures self-erasure in units of ocean depth. That is genius.
I don't dispute the beauty of it — but I want to hold on to the structural problem for just a moment longer.
Harmon reaches an impossible fork in the road, and Dickens names it with real precision.
If he comes to life and takes the inheritance, he is buying Bella. If he comes to life and rejects it, he is punishing her.
He cannot win within the system his father created — which is, I'd argue, the novel's central insight about inherited wealth.
And notice how that trap extends outward — to Wegg, to Venus, to everyone orbiting the Boffins' fortune.
Harmon ultimately turns Wegg's own scheming against him — watching, waiting, letting the deception run so the disappointment will be total.
"I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
The man who spent the novel as a shadow now deploys a shadow of his own. The symmetry is cold and exact.
What makes this plot machinery so remarkable is that Dickens was engineering it across nineteen monthly instalments — and he knew perfectly well readers would be ahead of him.
There is a remarkable moment in the postscript — the closest Dickens ever comes to an authorial confession — where he addresses this directly.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
He was not alarmed, he tells us. He trusted his audience to grant him patience.
And then he goes further — describing the larger ambition of the design.

"To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design."
'Always working itself out.' That is the phrase of a man who thinks in mechanisms — in looms, in patterns, in slow revelation.
The serialised novel is not a constraint. For Dickens, it is the instrument.
And yet — and this is what I love about him — he absolutely cannot resist showing off.
He says the ambiguity might 'in part arise out of some ingenuity in the story' — in part, mind you — with all the false modesty of a man who knows precisely how good he is.
The reader who thinks they've seen through the trick has only seen what Dickens wanted them to see.
That's the real conjuror's trick — and it's been sitting in plain sight for a hundred and sixty years.
Deception that knows itself — that might be the most Dickensian thing of all.
And it raises a question we haven't yet touched: how does a novelist hold tragedy and comedy in the same hand at the same moment?
That's where we're headed next — Dickens's comic voice, and what happens when the laughter curdles into something darker.

segments.title: Laughter and Darkness: Dickens's Comic Voice in Tragedy

utterances.text: We've been tracking the cunning beneath Dickens's plot — the disguises, the misdirections, the narrative sleight of hand.
But there's another layer to that craft — the way Dickens deploys comedy right alongside the darkest material, sometimes in the very same breath.
Oliver, this is very much your territory — the comic voice and what it's actually doing.
Thank you — and yes, this is the thing that makes Dickens genuinely difficult to perform, and genuinely thrilling when it comes off.
He absolutely refuses to keep his registers separate.
Take the Lammles' scene with Fledgeby and Georgiana in the opera box — a scene of pure, delicious social manipulation.
The Lammles essentially conduct a courtship on behalf of two other people, putting words in their mouths they never actually speak.
And Dickens lands the joke with one of those perfectly timed summary sentences.

"Through this device the two young people conversed at great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments, without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even that not to one another."
That last clause — "not to one another" — is a full comic cadence in six words.
It's also, if you think about it, a portrait of a society in which people relate to each other almost entirely through proxies and pretences.
And those proxies and pretences are doing real social work — that's what I'd want to add.
The Lammles aren't just socially awkward matchmakers — they're operators, harvesting these two young people for their own financial survival.
The comedy is the vehicle, but the payload is something much colder.
Dickens makes it funny so you're laughing before you've registered quite how predatory the arrangement is.
And he does the same thing — that exact same trick — with Pleasant Riderhood, though the tonal blend there is even more vertiginous.
She's introduced almost like a comic grotesque — the pawnbroker's daughter of Limehouse Hole who preys on sailors as a matter of instinct and training.
And then comes this magnificent passage where every ceremony of ordinary life is filtered through her bitter experience.
"Show her a Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular licence to quarrel and fight."
It's very funny — and then it isn't, at all, because Dickens explains exactly why she sees it that way.
Her father's idea of parental duty was — and I'm quoting now — "always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap."
The joke and the wound are inseparable — that's Dickens at his most characteristic.
I think Oliver has identified something very precise there, and I'd frame it slightly differently.
What Dickens is doing in the Pleasant Riderhood passage is what the great moralists have always done — he is asking us to judge, and then withdrawing the grounds for judgement.
We laugh at her cynicism about weddings and christenings, and then we discover that her cynicism is entirely rational given everything she has endured.
The comedy becomes, in retrospect, an indictment — not of Pleasant, but of us for having laughed without pausing to ask why.
Dickens was a greater moral artist than he was a social reformer, and this passage is evidence of it.
I'd push back on the separation there — the moral and the social are the same thing in this novel.
But where I think Edmund is absolutely right is on the withdrawal of grounds for judgement.
And nowhere does Dickens make that more devastating than in the Riderhood resuscitation scene.
The crowd gathers around Riderhood's drowning body with something very like compassion — he is briefly, in near-death, their fellow creature.
And then he comes back to life, and watch what Dickens does.
"As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him."
The symmetry of that sentence is surgical — warm against cool, soften against harden.
Our compassion, Dickens is saying, is entirely conditional — conditional on the other person not being too specifically, recognisably themselves.
I find that passage almost unbearably precise.
But I want to turn to a passage that seems to me the darkest thing in the novel, precisely because it wears no comedy at all.
Dickens's account of Bradley Headstone's descent into murderous hatred — it's an extraordinary piece of psychological writing.
He doesn't give us a villain struggling against temptation — and this is the key insight.
He gives us a man who is actively, perversely cultivating his own murderousness.
Dickens puts it with a terrible directness — the passage runs like this.
"If great criminals told the truth — which, being great criminals, they do not — they would very rarely tell of their struggles against the crime."
"Their struggles are towards it. They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not to recede from it."
"The bloody shore" — that phrase has the quality of a nightmare remembered in full daylight.
Dickens understood, two centuries before any formal psychology of it, that the appetite for violence can be a form of self-completion.
What's remarkable to me is that the same writer who gives us the Lammles' puppet-theatre courtship is capable of that.
And I don't think those two registers are as far apart as they look.
The Lammles are also people moving toward something — toward a goal they are prepared to use other people to reach, without compunction.
The comedy is the disguise — underneath, the engine is the same.
Dickens uses laughter to make you lower your guard, and then he puts his hand in your chest.
And the darkness in Bradley is inseparable from his class position — that's what I want to add before we move on.
He is a man who has clawed his way into respectability through sheer discipline — "tied up all day with his disciplined show upon him," Dickens says.
And then at night "he broke loose at night like an ill-tamed wild animal."
The self that respectable society has demanded he suppress is still there — and it is murderous.
That's not a coincidence — that's a diagnosis.
Comic ventriloquism in one passage, the anatomy of a murderer's will in another — and Dickens holding it all together in a single novel.
Daniel's point about class and suppression brings us, I think, to what may be the deepest question the book raises — about what this society is actually doing to the people inside it.
That's exactly what we'll be exploring next — the social fabric of Our Mutual Friend, and the human cost of what Dickens called, in effect, a civilization built on refuse.

segments.title: Industrial Society and Human Value: The Social Fabric Unravels

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Dickens uses comedy to hold darkness at arm's length — and sometimes to pull it closer.
But beneath the laughter, there is a society — industrial, stratified, and in Dickens's view, fundamentally broken.
And the city itself is part of that indictment.
There's a passage early in the novel where Dickens describes London in bad spring weather — and it is one of the great sustained insults in the English language.
He writes it as a list, which is how you build a comic rhythm — each item landing harder than the last.
Listen to how it starts:
"Such a black shrill city, combining the qualities of a smoky house and a scolding wife; such a gritty city; such a hopeless city, with no rent in the leaden canopy of its sky."
Three adjectives — black, gritty, hopeless — each with its own little sentence.
The comic simile — smoky house, scolding wife — lands first, and then "hopeless" arrives and the joke turns serious before you've noticed.
What strikes me is that this is not primarily social documentation — it is atmosphere as moral condition.
The city is black and shrill because the souls inhabiting it — Podsnap, Veneering, the whole Shares world — are themselves hollow and loud.
Dickens is doing something quite classical here — the pathetic fallacy pressed into ethical service.
The leaden sky is not a comment on industrial capitalism as a system.
It is a comment on what happens when men care for nothing beyond money and reputation.
That is a moral argument, not a political economy.
I'd say the moral and the political are not so easily separated here.
The men who care for nothing beyond money are not moral failures in a vacuum — they are the product of a specific set of economic arrangements.
And what Dickens shows us, if we follow the novel to its margins, is what those arrangements actually cost.
The Hexam household — Gaffer's dwelling on the riverbank — is described in terms that go well beyond poverty as a backdrop.
Dickens gives us a phrase that I think is one of the most precise in the novel:
"roof, and walls, and floor, alike abounding in old smears of flour, red-lead... and damp, alike had a look of decomposition."
Decomposition — that word does not simply mean rot.
It means the dissolution of what ought to hold together — shelter, safety, dignity.
The building itself is described as having a "rotten wart of wood upon its forehead" — which is grotesque, almost Hogarthian.
But the effect is not comic in the way Podsnap is comic.
There's no pleasure in it — it's an image of something used up and left to moulder.
Dickens's great skill is knowing exactly when to stop being funny.
I will grant that — the novel is quite clear-eyed about material misery.
But I am always cautious about reading Dickens as a systematic critic of institutions rather than a defender of individual human beings within them.

When he turns to the Poor Law — and he does so directly, in an authorial aside — what moves him is not the law as abstraction but the specific figure of Betty Higden, a woman choosing death over the workhouse.
That is a story about individual dignity — not about the machinery of capitalism.
But Dickens himself refuses that separation — that's the remarkable thing about this passage.
He steps out of the fiction altogether to defend his critique of the Poor Law in direct terms.
And what he says is extraordinary — this is not sentiment dressed up as argument.
He writes:
"I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised."
That triple repetition — "no law... no law... no law" — is not rhetoric for its own sake.
It is the structure of an indictment — the accumulation of evidence before the verdict.
And then he goes further, adding: "the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity — and known language could say no more of their lawlessness."
That final clause — "known language could say no more" — is Dickens reaching the limit of prose itself.
That phrase stops you cold.
The man who gives us Mr Podsnap and all his magnificent absurdity is also the man writing at the outer edge of what language can carry.
Both are the same writer — that's what makes him inexhaustible.
And I think that is precisely where his power resides — not in any particular programme, but in the sheer range of human experience he can hold simultaneously.
The grotesque comedy and the quiet devastation are not in tension — they are both expressions of the same moral seriousness.
Even when I resist his politics, I cannot resist his humanity.
A broken social fabric, and yet a novelist who keeps insisting — even at the limit of language — that something better is possible.

That tension between devastation and hope brings us to the question we've been circling all episode — whether this novel ultimately offers any kind of redemption, and what Dickens believes justice might actually look like.

segments.title: Closing: Transformation, Justice, and Dickens's Redemptive Vision

utterances.text: We've been tracing how Dickens anatomises a society that grinds people down — now I want to turn to the other half of his vision: whether anything, or anyone, gets redeemed.
Because Our Mutual Friend is not only a novel of corrosion — it's also, stubbornly, a novel of transformation.
And I think that is precisely where Dickens's moral imagination is at its most serious — and most moving.
Take Lizzie Hexam, whom we have not spoken of enough today.
She is, for my money, the novel's truest moral centre — a woman of the riverbank who achieves something extraordinary through love and self-discipline.
There is a passage in which she describes what Eugene's presence has meant to her, and it is as fine as anything Dickens wrote.

She says: 'I should lose a kind of picture of him — or of what he might have been, if I had been a lady, and he had loved me — which is always with me, and which I somehow feel that I could not do a mean or a wrong thing before.'
She carries him as an ideal — not a possession, but a moral compass she has fashioned from love.
That is not sentiment. That is moral philosophy in the mouth of a working woman.
It stops you cold when you read it aloud, that passage.
Because there's a double impossibility in it — the class barrier that makes the love impossible, and then the further cruelty that the very impossibility is what purifies her.
She can't have him, so she holds a vision of him — and the vision makes her better than she could have been otherwise.
And notice what Dickens does with her hands — the image he chooses to close on.
'They were coarse, and cracked, and hard, and brown when I rowed on the river with father, and are softened and made supple by this new work as you see them now.'
The body itself has been transformed. That's Dickens the performer — he makes you see the change in the flesh.
I don't want to seem heartless about Lizzie, because that passage is genuinely beautiful.
But I think we have to be clear about what transformation actually means for Dickens's working-class characters.
Lizzie's hands are softened — and that's presented as a gain, a refinement.
But those coarse, cracked, brown hands were the hands that kept her alive, that worked the river — and Dickens is not entirely comfortable with that labour.
His redemption for the poor tends to mean becoming less poor — less rough, less physical, more genteel.
The system is not challenged. The individual is elevated out of it, and that's supposed to be enough.
That is a fair charge to level at certain novels. I'm not certain it holds here.
Look at what Dickens does with Bella Wilfer's transformation — and look, crucially, at the mechanism he chooses.
Bella is not rescued by love alone. She is subjected to a deliberate moral experiment engineered by Mr Boffin.
And when she sees through it, her own description of what was done to her is quite remarkable.

She tells Boffin: 'you showed her, in yourself, the most detestable sides of wealth... and you took the pains to be the dearest and kindest fingerpost that ever was set up anywhere, pointing out the road that I was taking and the end it led to.'
A fingerpost. That word is doing enormous work.
It suggests Boffin is not merely kind — he is providential, almost allegorical, a guiding figure in a moral landscape.
That scene with Boffin and Bella is one of the great comic-sentimental coups in all of Dickens.
Because Boffin has been performing — marvellously, outrageously — as the corrupted miser for hundreds of pages.
And when the mask comes off, you feel both the relief and the sorrow simultaneously — relief that he was good all along, sorrow that goodness had to disguise itself so completely.
What I find piercing is Bella's own response — the confession she makes about her unworthiness.

She says: 'It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.'
She calls herself unworthy and she means it — and that is the proof she isn't.
And I'll grant Dickens that — there's genuine psychological acuity in the Bella arc.
The Boffin stratagem is also, let's be honest, a deeply strange critique of wealth — it says that in order to understand what money does to people, you have to perform its corruption.
That's a more radical idea than it first appears — that wealth's damage is only visible when the wealthy act out its worst tendencies in full.
Bella says Boffin showed her — and I love this phrase — 'the most detestable sides of wealth' precisely so she would recognise the road she was taking.
There is something almost Brechtian about that — wealth unmasked, held up for inspection.

The problem remains that the lesson is individualised — Bella learns, Bella changes, and the dust heaps pass to a decent couple rather than, say, being redistributed to those who actually worked them.
Redistribution is not the only measure of a novel's moral seriousness, Daniel.
Dickens understood what Burke understood — that social fabric is sustained not by structural rearrangement but by the cultivation of good character in individual souls.
What this novel argues, with great persistence, is that transformation is possible — that the dust of greed and self-interest can be refined, given the right pressure and the right love.
That is not a small thing. In fact, it may be the hardest thing of all to believe.
You know what strikes me, listening to the two of you circle each other?
Dickens held both of your positions simultaneously — and he never quite resolved the tension between them, and that is precisely why the novel lives.
He wanted to believe in individual redemption as fiercely as Edmund does. He was as angry at the system as Daniel is.
And he put all of that unresolved energy into his characters — into Bella's self-reproach, into Lizzie's impossible love, into Boffin's magnificent and rather lunatic stratagem.
The contradictions don't diminish the novel. They are the novel.
That feels like the right place to draw breath — and to close.
We've moved today through the Thames mud and the counting houses, through dustheaps and drawing rooms, through characters who corrode and characters who transform.
And what emerges, I think, is a novel of almost impossible ambition — one that tries to hold the social anatomy and the redemptive fable together in a single frame.
My warmest thanks to Edmund Leigh, for reminding us that moral imagination is its own kind of radicalism.
To Daniel Rosen, for keeping us honest about what the novel does and does not resolve.
And to Oliver Trevelyan, for hearing the music in every sentence and making sure we heard it too.
And to you, our listeners — thank you for spending time in the extraordinary, maddening, tender world of Our Mutual Friend.
It rewards every hour you give it.

c34:p0.text:
It was a foggy day in London, and the fog was heavy and dark. Animate
      London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing,
      and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose
      between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.
      Gaslights flared in the shops with a haggard and unblest air, as knowing
      themselves to be night-creatures that had no business abroad under the
      sun; while the sun itself when it was for a few moments dimly indicated
      through circling eddies of fog, showed as if it had gone out and were
      collapsing flat and cold. Even in the surrounding country it was a foggy
      day, but there the fog was grey, whereas in London it was, at about the
      boundary line, dark yellow, and a little within it brown, and then
      browner, and then browner, until at the heart of the City—which call
      Saint Mary Axe—it was rusty-black. From any point of the high ridge
      of land northward, it might have been discerned that the loftiest
      buildings made an occasional struggle to get their heads above the foggy
      sea, and especially that the great dome of Saint Paul’s seemed to die
      hard; but this was not perceivable in the streets at their feet, where the
      whole metropolis was a heap of vapour charged with muffled sound of
      wheels, and enfolding a gigantic catarrh.
c34:p0.summary: A richly detailed description of heavy London fog that obscures the city, making it simultaneously visible and invisible, with vivid imagery of gaslight, collapsed sun, and the metropolis transformed into vaporous chaos.
c34:p0.best_quote: Animate London, with smarting eyes and irritated lungs, was blinking, wheezing, and choking; inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither.

      over the bank and sunk it in the river. In and out among vessels that
      seemed to have got ashore, and houses that seemed to have got afloat—among

      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very

But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic

Yes, verily, my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, adapting your
      Catechism to the occasion, and by God’s help so you must. For when we have
      got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to
      relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their
      heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is
      a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance. It may not be
      so written in the Gospel according to Podsnappery; you may not ‘find these
      words’ for the text of a sermon, in the Returns of the Board of Trade; but
      they have been the truth since the foundations of the universe were laid,
      and they will be the truth until the foundations of the universe are
      shaken by the Builder. This boastful handiwork of ours, which fails in its
      terrors for the professional pauper, the sturdy breaker of windows and the
      rampant tearer of clothes, strikes with a cruel and a wicked stab at the
      stricken sufferer, and is a horror to the deserving and unfortunate. We
      must mend it, lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, or in its own
      evil hour it will mar every one of us.

But, the old abhorrence grew stronger on her as she grew weaker, and it
      found more sustaining food than she did in her wanderings. Now, she would
      light upon the shameful spectacle of some desolate creature—or some
      wretched ragged groups of either sex, or of both sexes, with children
      among them, huddled together like the smaller vermin for a little warmth—lingering
      and lingering on a doorstep, while the appointed evader of the public
      trust did his dirty office of trying to weary them out and so get rid of
      them. Now, she would light upon some poor decent person, like herself,
      going afoot on a pilgrimage of many weary miles to see some worn-out
      relative or friend who had been charitably clutched off to a great blank
      barren Union House, as far from old home as the County Jail (the
      remoteness of which is always its worst punishment for small rural
      offenders), and in its dietary, and in its lodging, and in its tending of
      the sick, a much more penal establishment. Sometimes she would hear a
      newspaper read out, and would learn how the Registrar General cast up the
      units that had within the last week died of want and of exposure to the
      weather: for which that Recording Angel seemed to have a regular fixed
      place in his sum, as if they were its halfpence. All such things she would
      hear discussed, as we, my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, in
      our unapproachable magnificence never hear them, and from all such things
      she would fly with the wings of raging Despair.

      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c31:p0.text:
The sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon all night long, was not
      conducive to sound sleep; but Rokesmith had some broken morning rest, and
      rose strengthened in his purpose. It was all over now. No ghost should
      trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin’s peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost
      should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of
      which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes
      in which it had no place.
c31:p0.summary: Rokesmith, having symbolically 'buried' John Harmon overnight, wakes resolved to maintain his disguise and protect the Boffins' peace by remaining dead to the world.
c31:p0.best_quote: No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place.

c31:p3.text:
Thus John Rokesmith in the morning, and it buried John Harmon still many
      fathoms deeper than he had been buried in the night.
c31:p3.summary: The morning's reflection deepens Rokesmith's resolve, further entombing his former identity.
c31:p3.best_quote: Thus John Rokesmith in the morning, and it buried John Harmon still many fathoms deeper than he had been buried in the night.

c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p99.summary: Harmon explains that they discovered Wegg's find through Venus, watched him closely, and deliberately prolonged his deception to maximize his disappointment.
c64:p99.best_quote: I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.
c67:p57.summary: Dickens explains that he intentionally created ambiguity about John Harmon's identity and asks readers to trust his artistic judgment and patience with the serialized format.
c67:p57.best_quote: I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.

c67:p58.text:
To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out,
      another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a
      pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and
      the most difficult part of my design. Its difficulty was much enhanced by
      the mode of publication; for, it would be very unreasonable to expect that
      many readers, pursuing a story in portions from month to month through
      nineteen months, will, until they have it before them complete, perceive
      the relations of its finer threads to the whole pattern which is always
      before the eyes of the story-weaver at his loom. Yet, that I hold the
      advantages of the mode of publication to outweigh its disadvantages, may
      be easily believed of one who revived it in the Pickwick Papers after long
      disuse, and has pursued it ever since.
c67:p58.summary: Dickens reflects on the difficulty of maintaining a secret subplot across serialized publication, defending the mode of publication despite its challenges.
c67:p58.best_quote: To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design.

c21:p117.text:
‘Alfred, my dear, Mr Fledgeby very justly says, apropos of the last scene,
      that true constancy would not require any such stimulant as the stage
      deems necessary.’ To which Mr Lammle would reply, ‘Ay, Sophronia, my love,
      but as Georgiana has observed to me, the lady had no sufficient reason to
      know the state of the gentleman’s affections.’ To which Mrs Lammle would
      rejoin, ‘Very true, Alfred; but Mr Fledgeby points out,’ this. To which
      Alfred would demur: ‘Undoubtedly, Sophronia, but Georgiana acutely
      remarks,’ that. Through this device the two young people conversed at
      great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments,
      without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even
      that not to one another.
c21:p117.summary: The Lammles create an entire opera-box conversation on behalf of Fledgeby and Georgiana through a series of attributed remarks, allowing the couple to be romantically 'entangled' without ever speaking to each other directly.
c21:p117.best_quote: Through this device the two young people conversed at great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments, without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even that not to one another.

c29:p3.text:
As some dogs have it in the blood, or are trained, to worry certain
      creatures to a certain point, so—not to make the comparison
      disrespectfully—Pleasant Riderhood had it in the blood, or had been
      trained, to regard seamen, within certain limits, as her prey. Show her a
      man in a blue jacket, and, figuratively speaking, she pinned him
      instantly. Yet, all things considered, she was not of an evil mind or an
      unkindly disposition. For, observe how many things were to be considered
      according to her own unfortunate experience. Show Pleasant Riderhood a
      Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular
      licence to quarrel and fight. Show her a Christening, and she saw a little
      heathen personage having a quite superfluous name bestowed upon it,
      inasmuch as it would be commonly addressed by some abusive epithet: which
      little personage was not in the least wanted by anybody, and would be
      shoved and banged out of everybody’s way, until it should grow big enough
      to shove and bang. Show her a Funeral, and she saw an unremunerative
      ceremony in the nature of a black masquerade, conferring a temporary
      gentility on the performers, at an immense expense, and representing the
      only formal party ever given by the deceased. Show her a live father, and
      she saw but a duplicate of her own father, who from her infancy had been
      taken with fits and starts of discharging his duty to her, which duty was
      always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap, and being
      discharged hurt her. All things considered, therefore, Pleasant Riderhood
      was not so very, very bad. There was even a touch of romance in her—of
      such romance as could creep into Limehouse Hole—and maybe sometimes
      of a summer evening, when she stood with folded arms at her shop-door,
      looking from the reeking street to the sky where the sun was setting, she
      may have had some vaporous visions of far-off islands in the southern seas
      or elsewhere (not being geographically particular), where it would be good
      to roam with a congenial partner among groves of bread-fruit, waiting for
      ships to be wafted from the hollow ports of civilization. For, sailors to
      be got the better of, were essential to Miss Pleasant’s Eden.
c29:p3.summary: Despite her predatory nature toward sailors and cynical views of life's ceremonies and relationships shaped by abuse, Pleasant Riderhood retains romantic dreams of escaping to distant islands.
c29:p3.best_quote: Show her a Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular licence to quarrel and fight.

c36:p28.text:
The short-lived delusion begins to fade. The low, bad, unimpressible face
      is coming up from the depths of the river, or what other depths, to the
      surface again. As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his
      lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him.
c36:p28.summary: The crowd's compassion evaporates as Riderhood's physical warmth returns and his character resurfaces, revealing their conditional mercy.
c36:p28.best_quote: As he grows warm, the doctor and the four men cool. As his lineaments soften with life, their faces and their hearts harden to him

c44:p1.text:
The state of the man was murderous, and he knew it. More; he irritated it,
      with a kind of perverse pleasure akin to that which a sick man sometimes
      has in irritating a wound upon his body. Tied up all day with his
      disciplined show upon him, subdued to the performance of his routine of
      educational tricks, encircled by a gabbling crowd, he broke loose at night
      like an ill-tamed wild animal. Under his daily restraint, it was his
      compensation, not his trouble, to give a glance towards his state at
      night, and to the freedom of its being indulged. If great criminals told
      the truth—which, being great criminals, they do not—they would
      very rarely tell of their struggles against the crime. Their struggles are
      towards it. They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not
      to recede from it. This man perfectly comprehended that he hated his rival
      with his strongest and worst forces, and that if he tracked him to Lizzie
      Hexam, his so doing would never serve himself with her, or serve her. All
      his pains were taken, to the end that he might incense himself with the
      sight of the detested figure in her company and favour, in her place of
      concealment. And he knew as well what act of his would follow if he did,
      as he knew that his mother had borne him. Granted, that he may not have
      held it necessary to make express mention to himself of the one familiar
      truth any more than of the other.
c44:p1.summary: Bradley consciously cultivates his murderous hatred, finding perverse pleasure in his rage. Dickens digresses to philosophize on the nature of great criminals: they struggle toward crime, not against it. Bradley fully understands his hatred and its inevitable consequences.
c44:p1.best_quote: Their struggles are towards it. They buffet with opposing waves, to gain the bloody shore, not to recede from it.

c12:p4.text:
When the spring evenings are too long and light to shut out, and such
      weather is rife, the city which Mr Podsnap so explanatorily called London,
      Londres, London, is at its worst. Such a black shrill city, combining the
      qualities of a smoky house and a scolding wife; such a gritty city; such a
      hopeless city, with no rent in the leaden canopy of its sky; such a
      beleaguered city, invested by the great Marsh Forces of Essex and Kent. So
      the two old schoolfellows felt it to be, as, their dinner done, they
      turned towards the fire to smoke. Young Blight was gone, the coffee-house
      waiter was gone, the plates and dishes were gone, the wine was going—but
      not in the same direction.
c12:p4.summary: London in poor spring weather is described as a shrill, smoky, gritty, hopeless city; Lightwood and Wrayburn retreat to the fire after dinner.
c12:p4.best_quote: Such a black shrill city, combining the qualities of a smoky house and a scolding wife; such a gritty city; such a hopeless city, with no rent in the leaden canopy of its sky

c3:p42.text:
The low building had the look of having once been a mill. There was a
      rotten wart of wood upon its forehead that seemed to indicate where the
      sails had been, but the whole was very indistinctly seen in the obscurity
      of the night. The boy lifted the latch of the door, and they passed at
      once into a low circular room, where a man stood before a red fire,
      looking down into it, and a girl sat engaged in needlework. The fire was
      in a rusty brazier, not fitted to the hearth; and a common lamp, shaped
      like a hyacinth-root, smoked and flared in the neck of a stone bottle on
      the table. There was a wooden bunk or berth in a corner, and in another
      corner a wooden stair leading above—so clumsy and steep that it was
      little better than a ladder. Two or three old sculls and oars stood
      against the wall, and against another part of the wall was a small
      dresser, making a spare show of the commonest articles of crockery and
      cooking-vessels. The roof of the room was not plastered, but was formed of
      the flooring of the room above. This, being very old, knotted, seamed, and
      beamed, gave a lowering aspect to the chamber; and roof, and walls, and
      floor, alike abounding in old smears of flour, red-lead (or some such
      stain which it had probably acquired in warehousing), and damp, alike had
      a look of decomposition.
c3:p42.summary: Dickens describes Gaffer's old mill-house in vivid detail: its rotting exterior, the low circular interior with rusty brazier and smoking lamp, wooden berth and steep stair, scattered oars and simple crockery, and its pervasive atmosphere of decay and damp staining.
c3:p42.best_quote: roof, and walls, and floor, alike abounding in old smears of flour, red-lead (or some such stain which it had probably acquired in warehousing), and damp, alike had a look of decomposition.

c67:p60.text:
In my social experiences since Mrs Betty Higden came upon the scene and
      left it, I have found Circumlocutional champions disposed to be warm with
      me on the subject of my view of the Poor Law. My friend Mr Bounderby could
      never see any difference between leaving the Coketown ‘hands’ exactly as
      they were, and requiring them to be fed with turtle soup and venison out
      of gold spoons. Idiotic propositions of a parallel nature have been freely
      offered for my acceptance, and I have been called upon to admit that I
      would give Poor Law relief to anybody, anywhere, anyhow. Putting this
      nonsense aside, I have observed a suspicious tendency in the champions to
      divide into two parties; the one, contending that there are no deserving
      Poor who prefer death by slow starvation and bitter weather, to the
      mercies of some Relieving Officers and some Union Houses; the other,
      admitting that there are such Poor, but denying that they have any cause
      or reason for what they do. The records in our newspapers, the late
      exposure by  The Lancet , and the common sense and senses of common people,
      furnish too abundant evidence against both defences. But, that my view of
      the Poor Law may not be mistaken or misrepresented, I will state it. I
      believe there has been in England, since the days of the  Stuarts , no law
      so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law
      habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of
      disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the
      country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known
      language could say no more of their lawlessness.
c67:p60.summary: Dickens defends his critique of the Poor Law as grounded in observable fact and ethical principle, arguing it is the most infamously administered law in English history.
c67:p60.best_quote: I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised. In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity—and known language could say no more of their lawlessness.

c42:p158.text:
‘I should lose some of the best recollections, best encouragements, and
      best objects, that I carry through my daily life. I should lose my belief
      that if I had been his equal, and he had loved me, I should have tried
      with all my might to make him better and happier, as he would have made
      me. I should lose almost all the value that I put upon the little learning
      I have, which is all owing to him, and which I conquered the difficulties
      of, that he might not think it thrown away upon me. I should lose a kind
      of picture of him—or of what he might have been, if I had been a
      lady, and he had loved me—which is always with me, and which I
      somehow feel that I could not do a mean or a wrong thing before. I should
      leave off prizing the remembrance that he has done me nothing but good
      since I have known him, and that he has made a change within me, like—like
      the change in the grain of these hands, which were coarse, and cracked,
      and hard, and brown when I rowed on the river with father, and are
      softened and made supple by this new work as you see them now.’
c42:p158.summary: Lizzie describes at length the spiritual and moral benefits Eugene's presence in her life provides: inspiration, motivation for self-improvement, a model for virtue, and a sense of purpose that shapes all her actions.
c42:p158.best_quote: I should lose a kind of picture of him—or of what he might have been, if I had been a lady, and he had loved me—which is always with me, and which I somehow feel that I could not do a mean or a wrong thing before.

c63:p54.text:
‘Then you ought to have said it, sir,’ returned Bella, giving him two
      pulls and one kiss, ‘for you must have thought and meant it. You saw that
      good fortune was turning my stupid head and hardening my silly heart—was
      making me grasping, calculating, insolent, insufferable—and you took
      the pains to be the dearest and kindest fingerpost that ever was set up
      anywhere, pointing out the road that I was taking and the end it led to.
      Confess instantly!’
c63:p54.summary: Bella passionately insists that Mr Boffin must have thought and meant to demonstrate how good fortune corrupts character, transforming his victim into something grasping and hard, and that he acted as a moral 'fingerpost' pointing out the danger.
c63:p54.best_quote: you showed her, in yourself, the most detestable sides of wealth, saying in your own mind, "This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in; but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking."

c63:p71.text:
‘O yes!’ cried Bella, covering her face with her hands; ‘but that I never
      shall be able to understand as long as I live. It is, how John could love
      me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could
      be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me
      a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife. But I am
      very very grateful.’
c63:p71.summary: Bella confesses her inability to comprehend how John could love her despite her unworthiness, and how the Boffins could invest such effort in her improvement and reformation.
c63:p71.best_quote: It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.
